doc.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Tap dancing learned from his sister Mary
summary: He explains that drummers of the era tap-danced and emceed in the theaters, and that his sister Mary taught him time-step and shim-sham, which helped his left foot on two bass drums.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: The biography in The New Grove Dictionary of Jazz lists that you learned tap- dancing, or were a tap-dancer with a barrelhouse pianist, Speckled Red. You said that you played with him. Did you also – is that an accurate account? Were you also a tap dancer?

All the drummers during that era – Jo Jones, for example, Buddy Rich – Steve Gadd was a Mouseketeer. They all tap-danced. They told jokes. Because when you played the theaters, you did everything. You were m.c. You had a dance routine. You had a dance routine called a b.s. chorus. It was nothing but a series of taps. That’s how Baby Lawrence, Teddy Hale, Bunny Briggs – that’s where all those guys came up, from the tap-dance era. My sister Mary – full sister – taught me how to tap-dance. She taught me the time-step first of all, and then the shim-sham-shimee. That’s how that started.
How old were you when she was teaching you this?
13 or 14. I did pretty good. That’s why two bass drums came in handy, because this left foot was strong.
